fact: Nepal's functional road classes: **National Highway (H)**, **Feeder Road (F)**, **District Road (D)**, **Urban Road (U)**.
detail: Separately classified by **terrain** — **Plain** (up to 10% cross slope), **Rolling** (10–25%), **Mountainous** (25–60%), **Steep** (over 60%) — which is what sets the geometric standards. The same class carries very different design speeds in different terrain.

fact: The **Nagpur road plan (1943–61)** adopted a **star and grid** pattern with a target density of **16 km/100 km²**.
detail: The successors: **Bombay (1961–81) square grid, 32 km/100 km²**; **Lucknow (1981–2001), 82 km/100 km²**. It also introduced the five-class hierarchy NH, SH, MDR, ODR, VR.

fact: **Home interview** is the O–D method for a **large urban area**; **registration number** for a **cordon** survey.
detail: Only the home interview captures **internal trips, trip purpose, mode and socio-economic data** — the variables needed to *forecast* trip generation, not merely describe today. It is expensive, so it is done on a **1–10% sample**.

fact: The four-stage transport model: **trip generation → trip distribution → modal split → traffic assignment**.
detail: An **O–D matrix** and **desire lines** (width ∝ trip volume, drawn between zone centroids) are the outputs of the survey that feed it. Desire lines show where demand actually is, which is not necessarily where roads exist.

fact: **Camber** values: **bituminous 2–2.5% (1 in 40–50)**, **cement concrete 1.7–2%**, **WBM/gravel 2.5–3%**, **earthen 3–4%**.
detail: A rougher, more permeable surface needs a **steeper** camber to shed water before it infiltrates. Too steep causes vehicles to drift toward the edge; too flat leaves standing water and causes **hydroplaning and pavement damage**.

fact: **SSD = lag distance + braking distance = 0.278Vt + V²/(254f)** with V in km/h.
detail: Reaction time **t = 2.5 s**; **f = 0.35–0.40**. **OSD = d₁+d₂+d₃** on a two-way road, and **ISD = 2 × SSD**. A **two-way single-lane road needs 2 × SSD** because both vehicles must stop.

fact: **Superelevation e = V²/(127R)**, and **e + f = V²/(127R)** allowing side friction.
detail: IRC design method: compute e for **75% of design speed with no friction**; cap at **e_max = 7%** (10% in hills without snow, 4% in urban areas). Then check that **f ≤ 0.15** at full design speed.

fact: **Summit curves are designed for SIGHT DISTANCE**; **valley curves for HEADLIGHT sight distance and COMFORT**.
detail: On a summit the road surface itself blocks the view; centrifugal force acts **upward**, opposing gravity, so comfort is not critical. In a valley the force acts **downward**, adding to gravity — felt as a jolt — and at night the headlight beam shoots up off the curve.

fact: **Grade compensation = (30 + 75)/R percent, maximum 75/R**, and **not applied to gradients flatter than 4%**.
detail: Because **curve resistance ADDS to grade resistance** — the tyres must be dragged sideways through the curve. **Hairpin bends** in NRS 2070: gradient **≤ 4%**, design speed 20 km/h, minimum radius **15 m**, e_max 10%.

fact: **Transition curve length**: the greatest of the **rate of change of centrifugal acceleration**, **rate of superelevation attainment**, and an **empirical (IRC) value**.
detail: The **spiral (clothoid)** is used because its **radius decreases linearly with length**, matching the driver's steering. Empirical: **L_s = 2.7V²/R** for plain/rolling terrain, **L_s = V²/R** for mountainous.

fact: **Extra widening on a curve = mechanical widening + psychological widening = nl²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R).**
detail: **Mechanical** widening is because the rear wheels track a smaller radius than the front (off-tracking); **psychological** because drivers keep further from the edge on a curve. Both are needed, and IRC gives tabulated values by radius.

fact: **Flakiness index: least dimension < 0.6 × mean.** **Elongation index: greatest dimension > 1.8 × mean.**
detail: Limits: **flakiness 25%**, **elongation 15%**, combined 40%. Flaky particles **break under compaction**, so an aggregate that passes every strength test in the laboratory can still fail in the road by changing its own gradation during rolling.

fact: Aggregate limits for **wearing surfaces: impact 30%, crushing 30%, Los Angeles abrasion 30%**; for other concrete **45% / 45% / 50%**.
detail: Impact tests **sudden shock**; crushing tests **gradual load**; abrasion tests **wear**. A wearing surface takes the stricter limit because it is directly exposed to wheel impact and braking with no covering layer.

fact: Bitumen tests: **penetration** (consistency, 100 g/5 s/25 °C), **ductility** (≥ 50 cm at 27 °C), **softening point** (ring and ball, 5 °C/min), **float** (hard bitumen).
detail: A **higher softening point means a harder, less temperature-susceptible binder** — needed in hot climates to resist **bleeding and rutting**; a lower one stays flexible in cold and resists **cracking**. IS 73:2013 moved to **viscosity grading (VG-10 to VG-40)**.

fact: **Marshall method** designs a bituminous mix using **stability, flow, air voids, VMA and VFB**.
detail: Optimum binder content is chosen at **4% air voids**, subject to minimum stability (**~9 kN**) and flow within 2–4 mm. Too much binder gives **bleeding and rutting**; too little gives **ravelling and cracking**.

fact: **Cautionary = triangle with red border**; **mandatory = circular**; **informatory = rectangular**.
detail: Two break their own rule deliberately, because they must be unmistakable even partly obscured: **STOP = octagon**, **GIVE WAY = inverted triangle**. Mandatory signs are **legally enforceable**; cautionary ones warn only.

fact: **PCU = Passenger Car Unit**, the standard unit for mixed traffic volume.
detail: Typical PCU factors: **car 1.0**, motorcycle 0.5, **bus/truck 3.0**, cycle 0.5, cycle rickshaw 2.0, tractor-trailer 4.5. Essential in Nepal and India where traffic is highly mixed — capacity in vehicles alone is meaningless.

fact: **Spot speed percentiles: 85th = speed limit**, **98th = geometric design speed**, **15th = lower speed limit**.
detail: **Time mean speed** is the average of speeds at one **place** over time; **space mean speed** is the average over a **length** at one instant, and is the **harmonic mean** — always the **smaller** of the two. Space mean speed is what enters q = k·v.

fact: **q = k · v** — flow = density × space mean speed, the fundamental relation of traffic flow.
detail: Flow is **maximum at the optimum density**, roughly **half the jam density** and at **half the free-flow speed** (Greenshields' linear model). Beyond that, adding vehicles **reduces** flow — the onset of congestion.

fact: A **collision diagram** shows the **type and manner of collisions at one location**; a **condition diagram** shows the **physical features**.
detail: Read together they turn an accident record into a **specific engineering remedy**: many rear-end collisions → improve SSD and advance warning; many right-angle → assign right of way; night concentration → lighting; wet-weather → skid resistance.

fact: **Flexible pavement** distributes load **grain to grain over a wide area**; **rigid pavement** by the **flexural strength of the slab**.
detail: So flexible pavements need a **strong subgrade** (design on **CBR**) while rigid pavements can bridge a weaker one (design on **modulus of subgrade reaction k**). Flexible: subgrade → sub-base → base → binder → wearing course.

fact: **CBR** is the ratio of the load to penetrate a soil to that for standard crushed stone, at **2.5 mm and 5.0 mm** penetration.
detail: Plunger 50 mm diameter, rate **1.25 mm/min**. Take the **2.5 mm value normally**; if the 5.0 mm value is higher, **repeat the test**, and if it repeats, use the 5.0 mm value. Soaked for **4 days** for design.

fact: **Design traffic in MSA (million standard axles)** with a standard axle of **80 kN**; **VDF (vehicle damage factor)** converts real axles by the **fourth power law**.
detail: Damage ∝ (axle load/80 kN)⁴, so a **60% overload does about 6.5 times** the damage. That is why **axle-load control matters more than any pavement design refinement** — one overloaded truck can undo a year's design life.

fact: Rigid pavement stresses: **load stress (Westergaard)**, **warping stress (temperature gradient)**, **frictional stress (uniform temperature change)**.
detail: **Critical combination = load + warping**, at the edge and corner. **Warping** comes from a gradient **through the depth** and is relieved by **warping joints**; **frictional** from a uniform change and is relieved by **expansion/contraction joints** — different causes, different joints.

fact: **Radius of relative stiffness l = [Eh³/(12k(1−μ²))]^(1/4).**
detail: It measures how far a slab spreads a load. Joints: **expansion 50–140 m**, **contraction ≈ 4.5 m**, **warping along the centreline**. **Dowel bars** transfer load across a joint while allowing movement; **tie bars** hold a longitudinal joint together.

fact: **Prime coat** on a **granular base** (penetrate and seal); **tack coat** between **bituminous layers** (bond); **seal coat** on the **finished surface** (waterproof).
detail: Rates: prime **7–10 kg/10 m²**, tack **2–3 kg/10 m²**. The sequence is: base → **PRIME** → binder course → **TACK** → wearing course → **SEAL**. A tack coat cannot substitute for a prime coat — it is too viscous to penetrate.

fact: **WBM (Water Bound Macadam)** uses coarse aggregate with screenings and binding material, **compacted with water**.
detail: **WMM (Wet Mix Macadam)** is graded aggregate premixed with water in a plant — more uniform, faster, and now preferred. WBM is laid in layers of **75 mm compacted thickness**, each with its own screening and rolling.

fact: Bituminous surfacings from thin to thick: **surface dressing → premix carpet → BM → DBM → BC**.
detail: **Surface dressing** is a waterproofing and skid-resistance treatment, **not a structural layer**. **BC (bituminous concrete)** is the dense, structural wearing course. **DBM** is the dense binder course. Choose by traffic and available funds.

fact: Pavement distresses: **ravelling, potholes, rutting, cracking (alligator, longitudinal, transverse), bleeding, corrugation, shoving**.
detail: Each points to a cause: **alligator cracking = fatigue from repeated load**; **rutting = permanent deformation, often excess binder or weak subgrade**; **bleeding = too much binder**; **ravelling = insufficient binder or poor compaction**.

fact: **Benkelman beam** measures **rebound deflection** to assess a pavement's structural condition and design an **overlay**.
detail: Higher deflection means a weaker pavement, hence a thicker overlay. Corrections for **temperature, seasonal variation and moisture** are applied to the characteristic deflection before overlay design.

fact: Highway alignment requirements: **short, easy, safe, economical** — and it must respect **obligatory points**.
detail: **Obligatory points through which the alignment must pass** (a bridge site, a mountain pass, an intermediate town) and **points to avoid** (a marsh, a lake, a religious site, unstable ground). In Nepal, **landslide-prone slopes and geological faults** are the critical avoid-list.

fact: Road width terms from narrow to wide: **carriageway → roadway (formation) → right of way**.
detail: **Carriageway** is the paved travel surface (**3.5 m per lane**, 3.75 m for a single-lane national highway); **roadway/formation width** adds the **shoulders**; **right of way** is the whole acquired land corridor, including drains and future widening.

fact: **Set-back distance** clears the inside of a horizontal curve so the required sight distance is available.
detail: **m = R − (R − d)cos(θ/2)** where θ = S/(R−d) radians. It is why obstructions — parapets, cut faces, vegetation, buildings — must be cleared on the inside of a bend, and why hill roads have benched cut slopes at curves.

fact: **Subgrade must be compacted to at least 97% of modified Proctor MDD**; sub-base and base to 98–100%.
detail: **Field density** is verified by **core cutter** or **sand replacement**. Compaction is done at or near **OMC** — too dry and the target density is unreachable, too wet and the soil shears and pumps under the roller.

fact: Rollers: **smooth wheeled** (granular, finishing), **pneumatic tyred** (bituminous, kneading), **sheep foot** (cohesive soil), **vibratory** (granular).
detail: **Sheep foot (pad foot)** works cohesive soil by kneading; **vibratory** rearranges granular particles and is far more effective on sand and gravel. Matching the roller to the material is the difference between reaching target density and merely passing over it.

fact: Signal design (Webster): **optimum cycle C_0 = (1.5L + 5)/(1 − ΣY)**, with L the total lost time.
detail: Green time is allocated **in proportion to the critical flow ratios y_i**. If **ΣY approaches 1** the intersection is at capacity and no cycle length will work — the geometry or the demand must change. Practical cycle lengths are **40–120 s**.

fact: **Rotary (roundabout)** design: **weaving angle ≈ 15°**, **weaving length**, and entry deflection to slow traffic.
detail: A rotary converts **crossing conflicts into merging and diverging** ones, which are far less severe. It suits **moderate** flows from **3–7 approaches**; at high volumes it locks up and a **signalised or grade-separated** intersection is needed.

fact: Hill road drainage: **side drains, catch water drains, causeways, culverts** — and drainage is the primary defence against landslides.
detail: A **catch water (intercepting) drain** above the cut slope diverts hillside runoff before it reaches the road. Most hill road failures in Nepal are **water-triggered**, so drainage maintenance matters more than pavement thickness.

fact: **Group Index** and **CBR** methods size a flexible pavement; **IRC 37** now uses **mechanistic-empirical** design.
detail: IRC 37:2018 checks two failure criteria: **fatigue cracking** (tensile strain at the bottom of the bituminous layer) and **rutting** (vertical strain at the top of the subgrade). Design period **15 years** for national highways, 10–15 for others.

fact: **Stripping** is the loss of adhesion between bitumen and aggregate in the presence of water.
detail: Worse with **hydrophilic (siliceous, acidic) aggregates like quartzite**; better with **basic aggregates like limestone and basalt**. Countered by **anti-stripping agents, hydrated lime or cement filler**, and by ensuring the aggregate is **dry** when coated.
